newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Bundestag postpones tax vote after row.
newsitem.headline: German Bundestag postpones tax vote after row.

text.p: Germany's lower house of parliament agreed on Friday to postpone a vote on abolishing a capital trading tax after a row broke out among deputies in the ruling faction of Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU).

The vote will now be held next week, after Chancellor Helmut Kohl meets opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leaders for a crucial tax summit on Monday which could pave the way for a compromise on a major shakeup of the German tax system.
The Bundestag, after a brief debate, approved a motion brought by the CDU/CSU faction to hold the vote later.

Christian Democrat deputies from eastern Germany -- where the tax is not levied -- wanted the abolition backdated to the start of this year, instead of January 1, 1998, in order to get a compensating share for local government from a turnover tax.
In the debate, speakers from the SPD and the opposition Greens said a change in the constitution -- which requires a two-thirds majority in the lower house -- was needed before the measure can pass.

SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss accused the ruling coalition of action which "clearly violated the constitution", and both he and the Greens demanded immediate financial compensation for municipalities in eastern Germany.
The capital trading tax is currently levied only in western Germany, but under a constitutional court ruling would have to be imposed automatically in the east if it is not abolished.

Wrangling over the abolition of the tax has dragged, but a cross-party deal on the issue could pave the way for progress the cross-party talks on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to slash 30 billion marks in taxes over the next two years.
